newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: USAID sees sound Czech economy, regulation needed.
newsitem.headline: USAID sees sound Czech economy, regulation needed.

text.p: The fundamentals of the Czech economy are sound and the government has finally discovered that proper regulation of capital markets is necessary to sustain them, a senior U.S. official said on Tuesday.

Speaking during a visit marking the closure of his agency's Czech office, U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) chief J. Brian Atwood said USAID was leaving Prague confident that a sound economic and political system had taken hold.

"The regulation side has to be put in place, but we believe that this is a fundamentally sound economy and even more importantly a fundamentally sound political system that is capable of making the corrections when the problems arise," Atwood told a news conference.

Analysts widely point to the lax enforcement of securities regulations as a major reason that many foreign investors have shunned the Czech markets and why many citizens have lost confidence in the government.
The centre-right government's approval ratings have fallen sharply in recent months amid a wave of reports on financial corruption, banking failures, and a downturn in the economy.
"The problem has not been that there is an absence of law, but there has been an absence of enforcement" on the capital markets, Atwood said.
The instability and poor macroeconomic data have led to a sharp drop in the value of the Czech crown in recent days, and the cabinet is in the process of a major reshuffle.

Recently consultants under the auspices of USAID, including former U.S. Securities and Exchange commissioner (SEC) Richard Smith, have been advising the Prague Stock Exchange in its efforts to establish an independent capital markets watchdog like the U.S. SEC.

After years of objecting to the creation of a strong market watchdog, Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik recently took the first steps toward creating a stronger securities watchdog.
